newsitem.title: FRANCE: Snow caused train breakdown in Channel Tunnel.
newsitem.headline: Snow caused train breakdown in Channel Tunnel.

text.p: Icy weather caused an ultra-modern Paris-London express train to break down in the Channel Tunnel at the end of a year of misery for the deeply indebted rail link, French railways said on Tuesday.

The train, carrying 469 passengers, ground to a halt near the middle of the 32 mile (51 km) tunnel on Monday when melting snow on its undercarriage caused a string of short-circuits in the engines, a spokesman for SNCF railways said.
It was stranded in the tunnel for almost three hours before it was towed out to the French side by a diesel engine in the latest setback for the tunnel's record of safety and efficiency.

The spokesman said temperatures in southeast England were minus 10 to minus five Celsius (14 to 23 Fahrenheit) with powder snow, creating condensation when the train entered the tunnel, where temperatures are between 25 and 30 Celsius (77 and 86F).

He said five of the eight motors aboard the Eurostar train were disabled, crippling the express train. SNCF, the French operator of the Eurostar service, was looking at ways to avoid a repeat of the fault but saw no need for major repairs.

"It's like a car that breaks down because the battery goes flat," he said, adding that a similar problem had briefly disabled a train in February. Travellers on the delayed service would get their tickets refunded.

Schedules returned to normal on Tuesday and Eurostar in London said the incident, and sub-zero temperatures across much of Europe, did not appear to have put off travellers, most of whom were going from London for New Year celebrations in Paris.
The breakdown was the first inside the tunnel since a fire on board a freight train last month injured 34 people and closed down the link for more than two weeks.
A rapid restart of most services after the fire by operator Eurotunnel prompted criticism from some British members of parliament and fire brigade trade unions.
Fears were swiftly reawakened when an empty train just outside the British end of the link caught fire after an electrical fault a fortnight ago.
For debt-laden Eurotunnel, 1996 has also been a year characterised by continuing financial headaches.

Although the company managed to settle an outline debt-for-equity swap with its 225 banks in October, creating a plan to pay off its 8.7 billion pound ($14.7 billion) debt mountain, long-suffering shareholders felt it gave them little.
The company's shares in London were set to end 1996 just under 80 pence, compared with their 1995 close of 87 pence.
While Eurotunnel stock has dropped 8.0 percent in the year, the London market as a whole has risen by about 12 percent.
In Paris, the firm's equivalent French shares were set to end 1996 at about 6.90 francs, just above their 1995 finish of 6.65 francs.
